newsitem.title: CHINA: China, HK agree on red chip stock offerings - Neoh.
newsitem.headline: China, HK agree on red chip stock offerings - Neoh.

text.p: China and Hong Kong securities regulators have reached a consensus on some issues related to red chip stock offerings in the British colony, Hong Kong Securities and Futures Commission Chairman Anthony Neoh said on Wednesday.
"The two sides have reached a consensus over the division of responsibility," Neoh told reporters at a securities conference in Beijing.
Red chip firms are China-controlled companies incorporated and listed in Hong Kong.
The issue of their regulation was sparked by the recent listing of GITIC Enterprises Ltd, a Hong Kong incorporated subsidiary of China-based Guangdong International Trust and Investment Corp.
The offering was nearly blocked when Chinese regulators objected to GITIC's failure to notify them prior to the listing.
"Red chips are Hong Kong companies, handled according to the Basic Law," Neoh said, referring to Hong Kong's future constitution that will take effect after China takes over the territory on July 1.
"China will govern the upstream companies," he said, referring to the Chinese parent firms. "Listings will have to be according to Chinese law."
Neoh said Hong Kong regulators decided to let the GITIC offer go ahead and then to deal with broader regulatory issues concerning such offerings at a future date.
The GITIC offer was a stunning success at nearly 900 times subscribed.
China and Hong Kong, which have been in talks on the issue of the regulation of red chips, would need to have further discussions on how to handle future cases, Neoh said.
"In future, these will be handled on a case by case basis," he said.

Securities industry sources said future listings of Hong Kong incorporated companies that have mainland-based assets will at least have to notify the China Securities Regulatory Commission, China's chief securities watchdog body.

They said it was still unclear how the two market regulators would manage the approval process but that mainland-based companies would at least have to coordinate with Chinese regulators for Hong Kong offerings of subsidiaries.
"This has been an operational issue. It requires time to get the right procedures," Neoh said.
